title: llm-d v1.0: State-of-the-art inference
content:
llm-d v1.0: State-of-the-art inference, ready for Day 2
llm-d v1.0 is here, and it is the project's most important release so far. In under a year and a half, llm-d has gone from a shared idea among a handful of contributors to the open standard for distributed inference, built by more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations: proven in production across every major accelerator, running on public clouds and sovereign on-prem fleets alike, and serving open models through both vLLM and SGLang. The founding vision, any model, any accelerator, any cloud, is now something you can deploy.
v1.0 is the release where that stack reaches maturity. llm-d already delivered hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box: prefix-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, and wide expert parallelism. v1.0 brings that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, upgrading without downtime, and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into your platform. Serving a frontier model fast is no longer the hard part. Running it reliably, for many tenants, through upgrades, under real load, is. That is what v1.0 is built for.
Delivering state-of-the-art performance
The defining goal of the 0.x series was reach: inference infrastructure that is not locked to one vendor, one cloud, or one engine. llm-d got there. It runs state-of-the-art inference across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs and Google TPUs, on managed clouds and sovereign on-prem clusters, and across open-source model servers including vLLM and SGLang, all behind the same routing and scheduling layer: prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism, and batch and async inference. The founding promise of any model, any accelerator, any cloud stopped being a slogan and became a deployment target.
The proof came from running it in production across clouds, accelerator vendors, and enterprises.
- Google Cloud builds the GKE Inference Gateway on the llm-d Endpoint Picker, cutting time-to-first-token by more than 35% in Vertex AI production while doubling its prefix-cache hit rate from 35% to 70%, and is integrating llm-d 1.0 into GKE across its TPU and NVIDIA portfolio.
- AWS runs disaggregated inference on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with llm-d, pairing prefix-cache-aware routing with prefill/decode disaggregation and NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter to report up to a 70% increase in tokens per second versus standard vLLM.
- DigitalOcean builds its distributed inference stack on llm-d for native GPU-type heterogeneity, serving the trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model across both AMD and NVIDIA hardware.
- Oracle Cloud Infrastructure runs llm-d on OCI bare-metal AMD MI300X with RDMA networking, and developed and validated the upstream AMD deployment guide on OCI.
- Tesla and Red Hat run Llama 3.1 70B on llm-d across AMD MI300X GPUs and, in a coauthored KServe case study, report a 3x increase in output tokens per second and a 2x reduction in time to first token from prefix-cache-aware routing.
- Prime Intellect integrates llm-d into its large-scale reinforcement learning stack, pairing the router with prefill/decode disaggregation and KV cache offload for multi-node rollouts.
- IBM Research self-hosts frontier open models on llm-d for coding agents and chip-design agents, serving up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents on 544 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and reaching a roughly 98% prefix-cache hit rate at about $0.11 per million tokens, around 11.5x lower cost than a proprietary stack.
- Mistral AI serves open models in production on llm-d as part of its regional inference offering.
- JetBrains runs llm-d behind Junie, its AI coding agent, using the scheduler's predicted-latency routing to keep responses fast under heavy agent load.
- Red Hat ships llm-d as the distributed inference stack in Red Hat AI, generally available on OpenShift and on managed Kubernetes including Microsoft Azure and CoreWeave.
Different clouds, different accelerators, different engines, one stack. These highlights come from a growing roster of more than 25 organizations adopting llm-d, and that breadth, proven in production, is the foundation v1.0 is built on.
Why Day 2 is hard
Getting a model to serve fast is Day 1. Keeping it serving, for many tenants, through upgrades, under unpredictable load, is Day 2, and it is where most inference stacks show their seams.
A production fleet carries mixed traffic: latency-sensitive interactive requests next to bursty agent workloads that reuse enormous amounts of context and spawn parallel work without warning. Priorities compete, and under load something has to give, so a premium tier has to stay protected while best-effort traffic absorbs the pressure. Upgrades and maintenance cannot mean downtime: you need to replace or fail over any component with no dropped requests and a cache that stays warm. Disaggregated deployments, which split prefill and decode across pools for efficiency, multiply the number of moving parts that have to roll forward together. Agentic traffic spends most of its compute on context rather than final tokens, so a stack that does not understand sessions and turns pays to recompute the same work again and again. And underneath all of it, inference has to be run like a service, with the observability to see what is happening and an owner who gets paged when it is not.
We know this because we run it. These are the requirements that showed up when the community, ourselves included, took llm-d from benchmarks to a standing production service. v1.0 addresses each of them directly.
Multi-Tenant Quality of Service
A shared inference fleet has to keep latency-sensitive traffic responsive while absorbing bursty, unpredictable agent workloads. v1.0 makes that a first-class property of the router through centralized flow control.
Priority- and fairness-aware flow control classifies every request by a flow key that combines a fairness ID (the tenant or workload) and a priority band, maintains a separate queue per flow, and dispatches by priority first, then cycles fairly across tenants within a band. Under saturation it does no-regret scheduling: it holds requests in the router rather than committing them to already-overloaded backend queues, so a burst from one tenant does not blow up latency for everyone else. Program-aware fairness lets operators express those policies per workload, and a probabilistic admission controller sheds load gracefully when demand exceeds capacity instead of failing hard. All of it now lives under a single flowControl configuration surface, and the defaults still mimic first-come-first-served, so existing deployments see no change until operators opt into multi-tenant policy. The result is that behind a single endpoint, a premium tier stays protected under load, measurably and not just by policy, while best-effort and batch traffic absorb the bursts.
Zero-Downtime Operations
Day 2 is where most serving stacks show their seams, and disaggregated serving multiplies the risk. v1.0 is built so upgrades and maintenance do not interrupt traffic.
Router high availability runs the Endpoint Picker with a hot standby that takes over scheduling if the active instance is replaced or fails, so routing never goes dark during a rollout. For disaggregated serving, DisaggregatedSet manages prefill and decode replicas as one logical unit: it gates readiness on a snapshot of the underlying pods and does revision-aware routing, so requests reach a prefill/decode pair only once both sides are fully rolled out and compatible. That makes coordinated, lockstep upgrades of a split prefill/decode deployment safe to run in place, instead of requiring a parallel fleet and a manual cutover. On the request path, a coordination layer in the router, consolidated into llm-d-router

report.summary: llm-d v1.0 ships the distributed inference stack's Day 2 features—multi-tenant QoS, zero-downtime upgrades, and agentic workload support—backed by production deployments at Google, AWS, Tesla, IBM and Mistral.
report.background: For the past two years the open-model inference story has been split in two: fast engines like vLLM and SGLang at the bottom, and Kubernetes plumbing at the top, with little standardised in between. Getting a single model to answer quickly ("Day 1") is largely solved; keeping a fleet serving many tenants, through upgrades, under bursty agent traffic ("Day 2") is not. llm-d emerged roughly eighteen months ago as a shared idea among a handful of contributors to fill that gap—a vendor-neutral routing and scheduling layer that sits above any model server and any accelerator. It has since grown into what the project calls the open standard for distributed inference, with 500+ contributors from 25+ organisations, spanning NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs plus Google TPUs, on public clouds and sovereign on-prem clusters. v1.0 is the release where that breadth is hardened into operational maturity.
key_points: Any model, any accelerator, any cloud is now a deployment target rather than a slogan. The same routing and scheduling layer runs across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs and Google TPUs, on managed clouds or sovereign on-prem fleets, serving open models through vLLM, SGLang or both—with prefix-cache-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch/async inference available out of the box.

Multi-tenant quality of service becomes a first-class router property. Centralised flow control tags each request with a fairness ID (tenant/workload) plus a priority band, keeps a queue per flow, and dispatches by priority then round-robin within a band. Under saturation it holds requests in the router instead of dumping them onto overloaded backends, with a probabilistic admission controller to shed load gracefully. Defaults remain first-come-first-served, so nothing changes until operators opt in.

Zero-downtime operations target disaggregated serving specifically. Router high availability runs the Endpoint Picker with a hot standby that takes over scheduling if the active instance fails or is replaced. DisaggregatedSet treats prefill and decode replicas as one logical unit, gating readiness on a pod snapshot and using revision-aware routing, so a split deployment can be rolled forward in lockstep in place instead of needing a parallel fleet and manual cutover.

Production results are the strongest evidence. Google Cloud's GKE Inference Gateway cut time-to-first-token by over 35% in Vertex AI production while doubling prefix-cache hit rate from 35% to 70%. AWS reports up to 70% more tokens per second on SageMaker HyperPod versus standard vLLM. Tesla and Red Hat saw 3x output tokens per second and 2x lower TTFT on AMD MI300X. IBM Research served ~3,000 concurrent coding agents on 544 H100s at about $0.11 per million tokens, roughly 11.5x cheaper than a proprietary stack.

The ecosystem has broadened well beyond hyperscalers. DigitalOcean runs a trillion-parameter model across mixed AMD and NVIDIA hardware, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure validated the upstream AMD deployment guide on bare-metal MI300X with RDMA, Prime Intellect uses it in large-scale reinforcement learning rollouts, Mistral AI serves open models regionally on it, JetBrains runs it behind its Junie coding agent, and Red Hat ships it as the distributed inference stack in Red Hat AI, generally available on OpenShift and managed Kubernetes including Azure and CoreWeave.
report.impact: The message to the AI industry is that inference competition has moved from raw tokens-per-second benchmarks to operational fitness—fairness, upgrade safety, observability and cost per token at fleet scale. For infrastructure teams, v1.0 lowers the barrier to running one shared, heterogeneous fleet for many internal tenants, which is exactly the pattern agentic coding and design tools demand: heavy context reuse, bursty parallelism, and strict latency tiers. The headline economics matter most: a ~98% prefix-cache hit rate at roughly $0.11 per million tokens shows caching and routing, not just GPUs, now drive unit cost, pressuring proprietary serving stacks. For developers, the payoff is a stable Kubernetes-native target above vLLM and SGLang rather than bespoke glue. Regular users should notice faster first tokens, steadier latency during traffic spikes, and fewer outages during upgrades.
report.tools: To follow up, start with llm-d itself (router, Endpoint Picker, DisaggregatedSet), which composes with vLLM and SGLang as model servers. NIXL handles KV transfer for disaggregated setups, while LMCache and llm-d's KV offloading layer are worth watching for cache economics. At the platform level, track the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension, Google's GKE Inference Gateway, KServe (see the Tesla/Red Hat case study), Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and Red Hat AI on OpenShift for a supported distribution.
